# Executive Summary

::: {.callout-note}
## Draft status
Written last, as an abstract of the sections that follow. Figures for corpus
composition and the model trade-off are generated from live project data; the
evaluation numbers are from the measured runs described in @sec-evaluation.
:::

The Ethics Navigator is a locally-hosted question-answering system that lets a
neurotechnology company interrogate the ethical and legal instruments that
govern its work — UNESCO's neurotechnology recommendation, the OECD's
responsible-innovation principles, the UN Guiding Principles on Business and
Human Rights, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and the
jurisdiction-specific regimes of the EU and California.

It is the successor to a rules-based assessment tool piloted at an external
practitioner workshop in early 2026. That earlier tool asked a fixed
questionnaire and returned red flags. Practitioners who tested it rejected it as
too rigid: they found the questions academic and leading, the scope confined too
narrowly to partnership review, and the whole exercise a poor fit for how they
actually work. The most frequently requested replacement was a conversational
interface — an assistant that could facilitate the process rather than
administer a form. This system is that pivot: from a fixed decision tree to a
grounded conversation over primary sources.

The system runs entirely on the user's own machine. Documents, questions, and
answers never leave it — a requirement, not a preference, given that the
questions a company asks an ethics tool are themselves commercially and legally
sensitive.

**Headline results.** Against a nine-case gold dataset, the system answers
**6 of 9** correctly with the shipped 4-billion-parameter model, in 180 seconds
of total CPU inference. On the hardest case — an open request to summarise every
principle governing responsible neurotechnology development — an independent
judge model scores the answer **9 out of 14** on a rubric of principles the
corpus actually states; the largest model tested reaches 14 of 14 on an earlier,
smaller version of the same corpus (@tbl-models). All three current failures are
retrieval failures rather than reasoning ones, and the report is explicit about
which, because the distinction determines what would fix them.

These numbers are lower than an earlier draft of this report claimed, and the
reason is itself a finding: the corpus had been silently indexed twice, and
every measurement taken while that was true has been discarded and re-run
(@sec-failures).

**Principal engineering finding.** Nearly every quality problem encountered
during development was a *retrieval* problem masquerading as a model problem.
Fixing document chunking doubled retrieval recall at fixed cost; adding
pre-computed per-document digests took the broad-synthesis case from
unanswerable to two-thirds coverage on the smallest model and full marks on the
largest. Changing the language model, by contrast, moved the headline score
comparatively little (@sec-tradeoffs). The corollary is uncomfortable and worth
stating plainly: because the failures are in retrieval, they are invisible in
the answer text, which stays fluent and well-attributed while being incomplete.

# Introduction

## Problem Statement

A neurotechnology company faces a proliferation of ethical and regulatory
guidance whose implementation pathways are, as practitioners put it, unclear.
The instruments are public, lengthy, and written for regulators
rather than founders. UNESCO's recommendation alone runs to over a hundred
thousand characters across nine principles, seven values, and twelve areas of
policy action; the EU AI Act is five times longer again.

The practical question a founder asks is not "what does Article 9 say" but
"what applies to *us*, and what must we actually do about it". Answering that
today requires either in-house neuroethics expertise — which practitioner
feedback identified as absent in most companies — or expensive external counsel.

The system addresses a narrow, tractable slice of this: **making the primary
sources directly interrogable in natural language, with answers grounded in and
attributed to the documents themselves.**

## Motivation

The motivation is documented rather than assumed. The predecessor tool was
tested by practitioners at an external workshop, and its shortcomings were
recorded in structured feedback.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Optional: chart the feedback themes
The report currently reports the feedback themes as prose and a table, which
needs no execution environment. To chart them instead, commit the exported
response CSVs to `report/data/` and add a figure chunk along these lines — note
this requires `jupyter` and `matplotlib`, which are deliberately *not* project
dependencies.

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

responses = pd.read_csv("data/workshop_feedback.csv")
# Code each free-text response against the theme list below, then:
#   rigidity / binary scoring · wants dialogue or AI facilitator · workflow fit
#   scope too narrow · Western regulatory framing · cannot replace humans
themes = responses["theme"].value_counts()
ax = themes.sort_values().plot.barh()
ax.set_xlabel("Responses mentioning theme")
plt.tight_layout()
```
:::

Five criticisms were reported back to the room, and they map cleanly onto design
requirements for a successor:

| Feedback finding | Design consequence |
|---|---|
| Questions read as academic and leading | Let the user pose the question; do not script it |
| UX friction, limited interaction options | Conversational interface, not a form |
| EU/Western regulatory framing may not translate globally | Explicit jurisdiction selection; global instruments always in scope |
| Scope confined to partnership review | Answer any question the corpus can support |
| Poor fit with day-to-day work | Run locally, answer on demand, no orchestration required |

The free-text responses were more specific still. Several asked for graded or
directional output in place of a binary checklist, and for prose and process
rather than yes/no answers. Others argued the tool should characterise a
partnership's risk exposure rather than emit red flags at the end. A number of
respondents converged independently on an assistant able to adapt as ethical
boundaries and technologies change.

Two cautions from the same feedback are treated here as binding constraints
rather than aspirations. First, that a tool of this kind does not remove the
need for education, collaboration, and human expertise. Second, that it should
not build new mechanisms where adequate ones already exist. The system is
therefore scoped as a *reference instrument* — it surfaces and attributes what the
governing documents say. It does not score partners, does not decide, and does
not attempt to replace counsel or an ethics advisory board.

## Scope and Objectives

**In scope.**

- Natural-language questions answered strictly from an indexed corpus of
  ethical and legal instruments.
- Answers attributed to the specific documents they draw on.
- Jurisdiction awareness: global instruments always apply; EU and California
  regimes are opt-in, so a Californian company is not advised out of EU law it
  is not subject to.
- Two question types: specific factual lookup, and broad synthesis across a
  whole document.
- Fully local execution, including the language model.
- User-supplied documents in addition to the shipped corpus.

**Out of scope**, deliberately, and consistent with the predecessor tool's own
stated boundaries and the practitioner caution against over-reach:

- Scoring, ranking, or red-flagging partners.
- Standalone decision-making, or any output framed as a decision.
- Legal advice or a compliance attestation.
- Replacing live discussion, an ethics advisory board, or counsel.

**Objectives.** The system is judged against three: (i) answers are *grounded* —
supported by the corpus and attributed to it; (ii) questions the corpus cannot
answer are *refused* rather than fabricated; and (iii) broad questions receive
*complete* answers, not a plausible-sounding subset. @sec-evaluation reports
performance against each.

# System Architecture

## High-Level Design

The system is three containers: a Streamlit front end, a Chroma vector store,
and an Ollama runtime hosting the language models. Nothing else is required,
and no network egress occurs after the initial model download.

The query path is: classify the question, retrieve from the matching pool under
the active jurisdiction filter, assemble a prompt within a token budget, and
stream a grounded answer back with its sources.

## Component Descriptions

### Tokenization and context budgeting

The system does not implement a tokenizer. Tokenization happens inside the
model runtime, and the application deliberately does not duplicate it. What the
application *does* own is **context budgeting**, and it is worth being precise
about the distinction because the naive approach fails silently.

Ollama defaults to a 2048-token context window regardless of the model's actual
capacity. Retrieved context that exceeds it is silently truncated — the request
succeeds, the answer is simply built on less evidence than intended. The system
therefore estimates prompt size (at roughly four characters per token, adequate
for sizing) and sets `num_ctx` explicitly per request.

The same budget governs conversation history. Retrieved evidence and the current
question are non-negotiable; whatever budget remains is filled with prior turns,
newest first. History is dropped oldest-first only when the prompt would
otherwise overflow, and the interface reports when it happens rather than
truncating invisibly.

### Language models

Four model roles are separated, but they run on three models: the classifier
shares the chat model rather than adding a third runtime download, since every
extra model is multiple gigabytes on a colleague's laptop.

| Role | Model | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Chat / answering | `gemma3:4b` | Fastest measured model on CPU, and it fails no gold case that the larger models also pass (@sec-tradeoffs) |
| Embedding | `nomic-embed-text` | Shared by ingestion and query, so both sit in one vector space |
| Mode classification | `gemma3:4b` (shared) | A two-way routing choice is easy; it does not justify a second multi-gigabyte download |
| Evaluation judge | `gpt-oss:20b` | Evaluation only, so no latency constraint applies — and deliberately a *different family* from the chat model |

The judge separation is a methodological safeguard: a model grading its own
output shares its blind spots, so scores would be inflated in exactly the cases
that matter. Generation runs at `temperature=0` with a fixed seed for
reproducibility, though bit-identical output is not achievable on this stack —
see @sec-failures.

### Retrieval

Retrieval is the component with the most design content, because it is where
nearly every observed quality problem originated.

**Two pools, not one.** Chunks are tagged `content` (verbatim document
excerpts) or `summary` (statements from a pre-built per-document digest).
Specific questions search excerpts; broad questions search digests. The reason
is measured, not stylistic: for the question *"summarise the legal and ethical
principles underlying responsible neurotechnology development"*, similarity
search over excerpts retrieved **0 of 3** known-relevant passages at *k*=50, and
required *k*=200 of 521 chunks — 38% of the entire corpus — to reach 2 of 3. An
abstract query matches abstract framing language, not the specific provisions
that actually answer it. Digests solve this by making each retrievable unit a
dense, self-contained statement.

**Line-aware chunking.** Chunks are packed on line boundaries rather than cut at
fixed character offsets. Fixed-offset chunking had placed six unrelated
definitions in one chunk, averaging its embedding across all six; the query
"what is cognitive liberty?" then failed to retrieve the passage that literally
defines it until *k*=50. After the fix, it retrieves at *k*=4.

**Jurisdiction filtering.** Every chunk carries a jurisdiction. Retrieval is
restricted to `Global` plus whatever the user selects, so EU regulation cannot
shape an answer for a company not subject to it.

### Digests

Digests are the mechanism that makes broad questions answerable. Each document
is read once, ahead of time, and reduced to a list of the statements it makes;
those statements are stored as `summary` chunks.

Two properties are deliberate. First, digest generation is a **separate,
explicit command**, never part of startup — it costs tens of minutes to hours of
CPU inference per document, and a colleague's first launch must not hang on it.
Second, digests are **files committed to the repository**, not merely rows in
the vector store. They therefore survive the vector store being rebuilt, ship
with the application so nobody regenerates them, and can be produced by any
model — including a frontier model via a web interface, which is how the
current corpus digests were produced.

That second property was learned the hard way: an early metadata migration
wiped the collection and destroyed hours of generated digests, because they
existed only inside Chroma. File-backed digests make that failure
unreachable.

### Guardrails

"Guardrails" here means a set of constraints on what the system will assert,
not a separate moderation library.

- **Grounding instruction.** The system prompt restricts answers to the
  supplied context and requires source attribution. It also, deliberately,
  instructs the model *not* to hedge when the context does support a conclusion
  — an earlier, stricter version caused the model to refuse questions it could
  actually answer.
- **Refusal.** Questions the corpus cannot support are declined. This is
  measured as a first-class test case, not assumed.
- **Determinism.** `temperature=0` and a fixed seed.
- **Jurisdictional scoping**, as above.
- **Visible routing.** The mode actually used is displayed with each answer, so
  an automatic misroute is visible rather than silently producing a worse
  answer.
- **Graceful degradation.** A broad question asked before digests exist falls
  back to excerpts *and says so*, rather than answering from an empty context.
- **Session isolation.** Uploaded documents are reachable only by the session
  that supplied them, and are purged automatically rather than on request.

### Local storage and privacy

All state is local: documents on disk, vectors in a Docker volume, models in a
second volume, conversation history in browser session state only and never
persisted to the vector store. After the one-time model download, the stack
requires no network access.

This is a functional requirement rather than a stance. The questions a company
asks an ethics tool — about a specific partner, a contemplated use case, a
regulatory exposure — are among the more sensitive things it could transmit.

**Two stores, not one.** Documents uploaded at runtime are confidential in a way
the reference corpus is not: the corpus is published international instruments,
while an upload may be a partner's unreleased charter or a draft agreement. They
are therefore kept in a separate, ephemeral Chroma collection rather than
alongside the corpus, and three properties follow from that separation:

- **Nothing is written to disk.** Uploaded bytes are read, extracted, chunked,
  embedded and dropped. An earlier version saved each upload into the documents
  directory so it would survive restarts — which, for confidential material,
  is precisely the wrong behaviour: the file would outlive every purge and be
  re-indexed into the *permanent* corpus on the next startup.
- **Removal is a collection-level delete.** Purging drops the whole collection
  rather than deleting by filter. A filter can be wrong and spare a chunk; a
  dropped collection cannot reach corpus or digest chunks at all. This matters
  because an earlier metadata migration destroyed hours of generated digests by
  wiping a shared collection — the structure now makes that class of mistake
  unreachable rather than merely discouraged.
- **Purging does not depend on the user remembering.** Streamlit has no
  session-end hook — a closed browser tab never reaches the server — so an
  explicit control alone would strand documents whenever someone simply walked
  away. Three triggers overlap instead: on application start, on an age-based
  sweep that runs on every interaction, and on an explicit end-session action.

Retrieval treats the two stores differently on purpose. Uploaded chunks carry no
jurisdiction filter, because a user's own material is always in scope rather than
an instrument that binds in particular places; and they are always searched as
content, because a document that exists only for the length of a session never
has a digest built for it. Answers label which retrieved passages came from an
upload, so material the user supplied is not presented with the same standing as
an indexed instrument.

### Containerization

Three services under Docker Compose: `app` (Streamlit), `chroma`, and `ollama`.
Named volumes persist models and vectors; `data/documents` is bind-mounted so
documents can be added from the host. Models are pulled automatically on first
run, so `docker compose up --build` is the only command a new user issues.

### Frontend

A single-page Streamlit chat interface. The sidebar lists indexed documents by
title, grouped by jurisdiction, with a selector for where the user operates.
Answers stream token-by-token, followed by the mode used, the retrieved sources,
and a copy-to-clipboard control for pasting into the user's own documents.

# Evaluation {#sec-evaluation}

## Yardstick

Evaluation is deliberately split by *stage*, because a drop in end-to-end
answer quality is otherwise unattributable — retrieval and generation fail for
different reasons and have different remedies.

| Layer | What it measures | Cost | Where |
|---|---|---|---|
| Retrieval eval | Does the known-correct passage reach the model at all? | Seconds, no LLM | `evals/retrieval.py` |
| Answer eval | Is the answer correct, per case-specific criteria? | Minutes | `evals/run.py` |
| Regression tests | Does the pipeline still behave? | ~5 min, small model | `tests/` |

The gold dataset lives in `evals/dataset.py` and is the single source of truth;
graders live in `evals/graders.py`. Both runners consume the same definitions,
so a regression test and an eval score cannot disagree about what "correct"
means. Every expected answer was verified against the document text before being
recorded.

Each case carries the jurisdiction selection it should be answered under, which
makes scope discipline a graded property rather than an assumed one. Two cases
exist only to test it: each asks a question answerable *only* from a
jurisdiction-specific statute that is indexed but deliberately not selected. The
correct behaviour is refusal, and the interesting result is that the two do not
behave alike — which is what makes them worth keeping as separate cases rather
than one.

Three grader types are used. `refusal` asks the judge model whether an answer
declines to answer. `contains` checks that required content appears, with
synonym groups so that phrasing is not over-constrained. `judge` asks the judge
model, one rubric item at a time, whether the answer conveys a specific
principle — a narrow binary question a model answers reliably, unlike an
open-ended "is this good?".

Refusal grading was originally a list of refusal phrases and became
judge-based for a reason worth recording: three different chat models declined
the same unanswerable question in three phrasings the list did not contain, so
the grader reported failures on answers that were exactly right. A refusal is a
semantic property, not a lexical one, and matching strings was measuring the
wrong thing. The regression tests in `tests/` deliberately keep their own
phrase-based check instead, so that the fast gate stays fast and free of a
dependency on a second model.

## Results by Mode

| Case | Grader | Mode | Result | Time | Note |
|---|---|---|:--:|--:|---|
| `cake-refusal` | refusal | Question answering | **PASS** | 20s | Correctly declines; no cake document indexed |
| `time-off-right` | contains | Question answering | **PASS** | 13s | Cites UDHR Article 24 |
| `oecd-due-regard` | contains | Question answering | **FAIL** | 13s | Boilerplate outranks the provision — @sec-failures |
| `cognitive-liberty` | contains | Question answering | **PASS** | 7s | Exact definition returned |
| `neural-data` | contains | Question answering | **PASS** | 11s | Definition with all required elements |
| `equitable-access` | contains | Question answering | **PASS** | 14s | Names LMICs explicitly |
| `gdpr-without-eu-selected` | refusal | Question answering | **FAIL** | 13s | Answered from a global instrument instead of declining |
| `ccpa-without-california-selected` | refusal | Question answering | **PASS** | 10s | Correctly declines; California not selected |
| `broad-principles` | judge | Broad principles | **FAIL** | 79s | 9/14 rubric coverage |

: End-to-end results, nine gold cases, chat model `gemma3:4b`, 180s total. {#tbl-results}

**Question-answering mode: 6 of 8.** Specific factual questions are answered
from verbatim excerpts at *k*=4, and the two failures are instructive in
different ways. `oecd-due-regard` is the long-standing boilerplate defect
described below. `gdpr-without-eu-selected` is newer and more interesting: the
user has not opted into the EU jurisdiction, so GDPR chunks are correctly
filtered out of retrieval, and the honest response is to say the question cannot
be answered in the current scope. Instead the model answered the consent
question from UNESCO's general treatment of consent — accurately attributed, and
still wrong, because it silently substitutes a global instrument for the statute
that was actually asked about.

That case passed in an earlier run and fails now, on the same model at
temperature 0 with a fixed seed. Nothing about the model changed; the retrieved
context did, and with it the model's choice between disclaiming and answering
anyway. **Refusal is therefore not a stable property of the system.** It is a
behaviour that emerges from whatever the retriever returned, which is precisely
why it is graded as a case rather than assumed.

**Broad-principles mode: 9 of 14.** The open synthesis question — the one the
system was least able to answer before digests existed — covers nine of the
fourteen principles the corpus states. For scale, the same question answered by
naive retrieval covered roughly a third of them, so digests remain the single
largest quality improvement made. But the gap is real, and its content matters
more than its size: the misses include the protection of neural data and mental
privacy, non-discrimination and neurodiversity, accountability and remedy, the
interests of children and future generations, and prohibition of misuse for
social control. Those are not peripheral principles, and an answer omitting them
does not read as incomplete.

## Common Failure Modes {#sec-failures}

**Retrieval loses to boilerplate.** The oldest of the three failures,
`oecd-due-regard`, asks what societal values the OECD document says should be
shown due regard. The answer is one clause of principle 1(d). The query names
the document — "the OECD document" — and that phrase matches the OECD's *front
and back matter* far more strongly than its provisions. All seven top-ranked
chunks are the "About the OECD" section, the preamble's list of prior
instruments, the Compendium blurb, and the "please cite this document as" line.
The provision never enters the context — the nearest boilerplate chunk sits at
distance 0.253, comfortably inside a *k*=4 window.

This failure reproduces **identically across four different chat models**, which
is the strongest available evidence that it is a retrieval defect rather than a
reasoning one. The remedy is to strip boilerplate sections at ingestion — now
straightforward, since the markdown conversion gave every document real
headings.

**Grader brittleness can masquerade as system failure.** An initial scorecard
read 4 of 7. Two of those three failures were defects in the *graders*: the
chat model wrote "self‑determination" with a non-breaking hyphen, defeating an
ASCII substring match on an answer that was exactly correct; and it refused the
cake question with a phrasing absent from the refusal-phrase list. Both were
real bugs, but in the measuring instrument. This is recorded here because the
failure mode is insidious: an eval that under-reports looks like diligence. The
first was fixed with a shared text normaliser applied to both sides of every
comparison; the second by replacing phrase matching with the judge.

**A prior turn's conclusion can override the current turn's evidence.** The
system re-retrieves and rebuilds its context on every turn, so each answer
should rest only on what that turn retrieved. It does not. Asked a question
about one jurisdiction's law, then the same question with that jurisdiction out
of scope, the model repeats its earlier conclusion — correctly refusing at the
start of the answer, then restating the previous turn's finding anyway. Seeding
a single prior answer into an otherwise empty history reproduces it on demand;
the same question asked with no history refuses cleanly and completely.

The cause is conversational, not retrieval: retrieval correctly excludes the
out-of-scope document, and the model is pattern-completing against its own
previous turn. It is recorded here because the obvious reading — "the model
hallucinated a citation" — is wrong and would send a fix to the wrong
component, and because the grounding instruction's deliberate anti-hedging
clause (@sec-failures, *Guardrails*) is what gives a stale conclusion licence to
persist.

**Determinism is behavioural, not bit-exact.** At `temperature=0` the model
makes the same answer-versus-refuse decision every time, but token-identical
output is not achievable: multithreaded floating-point reductions in the
inference backend are non-associative, so near-tied logits can flip between
runs. The regression tests assert the former and not the latter.

**More context is not monotonically better.** Retrieval recall plateaus between
*k*=8 and *k*=30 on this corpus — every chunk past the eighth adds cost without
adding evidence. Measured end-to-end, *k*=30 produced a *less* complete answer
than *k*=12, consistent with the "lost in the middle" effect [@liu2023lostmiddle].
This is why the modes retrieve 4 and 12 chunks rather than as many as fit.

**Corpus growth dilutes broad retrieval.** With seven documents' digests
competing, the broad case needs a larger *k* to surface the same passages it
found when two documents were indexed. It is a scaling pressure to watch: the
tuned constants were fitted to a corpus that has since roughly tripled.

**A tuned *k* silently expires as the corpus grows.** The same pressure reaches
question-answering mode, where it is easier to miss because the answers stay
fluent. Asked what counts as sensitive data under the California statute — with
California correctly selected, and the mode correctly routed — the system
returns four passages, none of which answer the question: two from the UNESCO
recommendation and two from the statute's own procedural and administrative
sections. The passage that does answer it, the enumerated definition that also
contains the statute's neural-data clause, ranks **fourteenth** at a distance of
0.289, while the *k*=4 cutoff falls at 0.257. Of the thirteen chunks ahead of
it, eight are UNESCO and five are CCPA boilerplate — so this is not simply one
document crowding out another, but the general instrument and the target
statute's own front matter both scoring closer to the question than the clause
that answers it.

The model then answers from what it was given: it correctly reports that the
context does not define the term, and reasons toward a conclusion from the
general instrument instead. Nothing in the pipeline is broken; *k*=4 was
measured to retrieve every known-good passage on a four-document corpus, and
that measurement has quietly stopped holding at seven. This is a specific
argument for treating retrieval constants as measurements with an expiry date
rather than as configuration, and for adding a gold case per document as the
corpus grows — the retrieval eval exists precisely to make this cheap to detect.

**One document in two formats is two documents to the index.** The source PDFs
were added to the document folder alongside the converted markdown, so that the
unaltered originals sat next to the text actually being indexed. Ingestion
walked the folder file by file and indexed both: the collection went from 3,630
content chunks to 6,759, and every digest existed twice under the same content
hash. Retrieval still worked and answers still read correctly, which is what
made it dangerous — the only visible symptom was a chunk count that no longer
matched the one recorded here.

The cost is paid in *distinct* evidence. At a fixed *k*, half the retrieved
chunks can be duplicates of the other half, so the effective context is smaller
than the parameter says, and a document stored twice gets two votes on every
query. The registry in `rag/corpus.py` had in fact already settled the right
rule — a document's identity is its filename *stem*, so that swapping formats
cannot change its title or jurisdiction — but ingestion never consulted that
rule and worked per filename instead. The fix resolves each stem to a single
file before anything is read, preferring markdown because the conversion carries
the headings chunking depends on. The existing prune-what-is-no-longer-on-disk
path then removed the duplicates without a rebuild.

The general lesson is about where an invariant lives. Stating it in one module
does not enforce it in another; it held wherever `corpus.py` was consulted and
failed in the one place that did the indexing. This is also why the corpus
statistics in this report are quoted as a check rather than as trivia: the
discrepancy is what surfaced the bug, and every measurement taken while the
duplication was present was discarded and re-run.

## Trade-offs {#sec-tradeoffs}

| Model | Size (GB) | Adjusted pass | Broad coverage | Total time (s) |
|---|--:|:--:|:--:|--:|
| `gpt-oss:20b` | 13.0 | 6/7 | **14/14** | 772 |
| `mistral-nemo:12b` | 7.1 | 5/7 | 13/14 | 713 |
| `llama3:8b` | 4.7 | 5/7 | 10/14 | 535 |
| `gemma3:4b` *(default)* | 3.3 | 5/7 | 12/14 | **306** |

: Chat model comparison, measured on the seven-case gold set that preceded the jurisdiction-scoping cases. Retained as the comparison that settled the model choice; it is not directly comparable to the current scorecard (@tbl-results), which grades nine cases. "Adjusted" corrects only for confirmed grader gaps, not genuine content misses. {#tbl-models}

**Model size versus latency, and why the smallest model won.** `gemma3:4b` runs
the suite in 40% of the time of `gpt-oss:20b`, and — the decisive point — it
fails no case that `gpt-oss:20b` also passes. The `oecd-due-regard` failure is
identical across all four models, which is what identifies it as a retrieval
defect rather than a reasoning one.

That combination inverts the usual instinct to default to the largest model that
fits. Where the biggest model's advantage shows up only on a dimension the
system does not depend on, its cost is paid on every single query while its
benefit is never collected. On CPU inference that cost is not marginal: it is
the difference between an answer arriving in seconds and in minutes. The larger
model is retained for the evaluation judge, where the same latency simply does
not apply.

A related decision was considered and rejected: letting the user pick the model.
Exposing the choice would reliably push users toward the largest option — it
reads as the safest — and then strand them with latency they did not
anticipate and cannot diagnose. A single measured default with a manual
override in an *Advanced* panel keeps that escape hatch without making every
user answer a question they have no basis to answer.

**CPU inference is the binding constraint.** With no GPU, answers take tens of
seconds to a few minutes. Thread count was tested directly and is *not* a
usable lever: forcing all sixteen logical cores was 2.1× *slower* than the
runtime's own auto-detection, because the two SMT threads per physical core
contend for the same execution units. There is no free configuration win here.

**Digest generation cost versus coverage.** Digests are what make broad
questions work, and they are expensive: the EU AI Act alone was estimated at
roughly thirteen hours of local CPU inference. The resolution was to decouple
generation from the application — digests are portable files that can be
produced anywhere, by any model, and committed. Local generation remains
supported for users who cannot use an external model, at a cost in time rather
than in capability.

**Local-only versus quality.** Running a 4-billion-parameter model on a laptop
CPU costs real answer quality relative to a frontier model, and the measurements
above put a number on part of that gap. This is accepted deliberately: the
confidentiality of the questions is the system's reason for existing, and an
architecture that sent them elsewhere would not be the same product. The
ordering is explicit — local execution is not negotiable, latency is the
variable that absorbs the cost, and context budget sits between the two.

**Multi-query retrieval: a rejected approach.** Decomposing a broad question
into targeted sub-queries was implemented and measured. It produced no recall
improvement, ran roughly 400× slower than single-query retrieval, and generated
sub-queries containing vocabulary absent from the corpus. It is retained in the
codebase but disabled by default. It is recorded here because the negative
result is informative: the fix for broad questions was better *source
material* (digests), not cleverer querying.

# Appendix: Corpus

| Instrument | Jurisdiction | Adopted |
|---|---|--:|
| Universal Declaration of Human Rights [@un1948udhr] | Global | 1948 |
| UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights [@un2011guiding] | Global | 2011 |
| OECD Recommendation on Responsible Innovation in Neurotechnology [@oecd2019neurotech] | Global | 2019 |
| UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Neurotechnology [@unesco2025neurotech] | Global | 2025 |
| EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) [@eu2016gdpr] | European Union | 2016 |
| EU Artificial Intelligence Act [@eu2024aiact] | European Union | 2024 |
| California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) [@ccpa2018] | California | 2018 |

: Indexed corpus. Global instruments always apply; jurisdiction-specific instruments are opt-in. {#tbl-corpus}

The indexed corpus comprises **3,630 content chunks** and **173 digest chunks**
across seven instruments. All seven are indexed from markdown, with the original
PDFs retained alongside them for provenance but deliberately not indexed
(@sec-failures); conversion was necessary rather than cosmetic, as extraction
from the Official Journal
typesetting of the GDPR corrupted roughly one word in four
(`ar ticle`, `p aragraph`, `author ised`), which would have made that document
effectively unsearchable.
